articles.summary:

On November 27, the world marks the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage – a chance to end a practice that robs children of their childhood and prospects. A study published this month, covering women across 117 countries, found that legal guarantees of pre-primary education were associated with higher rates of school completion among girls and lower rates of child marriage and adolescent childbearing. Domestically, it has guaranteed 13 years of free education, from pre-primary through secondary, since 2023 and banned child marriage in 2024.International law needs to catch up. The Convention on the Rights of the Child neither explicitly recognizes a right to early childhood care and education nor guarantees free pre-primary and secondary education for all. Sierra Leone, the Dominican Republic, Bulgaria and ten other countries are therefore advancing a new Optional Protocol to close these gaps. A binding commitment would strengthen accountability and drive national reforms. Negotiations on this proposed treaty will continue in October 2027.On this inaugural International Day, Sierra Leone, supported by 14 countries, will bring diplomats, experts, and child advocates together in Geneva. Investing in free education advances girls’ rights, dignity, and futures – and is a decisive step towards ending child marriage. By supporting the Optional Protocol at the United Nations, states will be making a clear statement that they stand against child marriage and are committed to delivering a freer and fairer world for girls.
articles.content:
Click to expand Image A student poses for a portrait in the classroom of her school in Koidu, Kono district, Sierra Leone, on November 24, 2020. © 2020 AP Photo/Leo Correa

On November 27, the world marks the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage – a chance to end a practice that robs children of their childhood and prospects. Every year, 12 million girls are married before 18 – that’s one every three seconds.

Free education is a powerful tool to help prevent it. UNICEF estimates that if all girls completed secondary education, it could cut child marriage by two-thirds. Yet school fees and indirect costs — uniforms, transport, books, examinations — force girls out of school and into early marriage. Free secondary education helps keep girls in school through adolescence, when the risk of child marriage is greatest. Evidence from 14 African countries shows that making lower secondary education free and compulsory raised girls’ educational attainment by 1.6 years.

And prevention needs to start earlier. A study published this month, covering women across 117 countries, found that legal guarantees of pre-primary education were associated with higher rates of school completion among girls and lower rates of child marriage and adolescent childbearing. Yet UNESCO reports that only 68 percent of countries and 46 percent of low-income countries legally guarantee tuition-free pre-primary education.

Free education from pre-primary through secondary forms a continuous pathway to opportunity and empowerment.

Sierra Leone shows what political leadership can achieve on both fronts. Its First Lady spearheaded this International Day, while its education ministers and diplomats have championed a new treaty on free education at the United Nations. Domestically, it has guaranteed 13 years of free education, from pre-primary through secondary, since 2023 and banned child marriage in 2024.

International law needs to catch up. The Convention on the Rights of the Child neither explicitly recognizes a right to early childhood care and education nor guarantees free pre-primary and secondary education for all. Sierra Leone, the Dominican Republic, Bulgaria and ten other countries are therefore advancing a new Optional Protocol to close these gaps. A binding commitment would strengthen accountability and drive national reforms. Negotiations on this proposed treaty will continue in October 2027.

On this inaugural International Day, Sierra Leone, supported by 14 countries, will bring diplomats, experts, and child advocates together in Geneva. Investing in free education advances girls’ rights, dignity, and futures – and is a decisive step towards ending child marriage. By supporting the Optional Protocol at the United Nations, states will be making a clear statement that they stand against child marriage and are committed to delivering a freer and fairer world for girls.

It provides substantial evidence and examples, including Sierra Leone's leadership and international treaty efforts, demonstrating a real and inspiring positive change with potential large-scale benefits.
articles.personality_title: Free education helps stop child marriage, says new global effort
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Every year, 12 million girls around the world are married before they turn 18. This practice, called child marriage, takes away their childhood and chances to learn and grow. To tackle this, November 27 has been named the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage.

**What happened** – Experts say that free education is a key way to reduce child marriage. If all girls finished secondary school, child marriage could drop by two-thirds. But many families cannot afford school costs like fees, uniforms, or books. Some countries, like Sierra Leone, have started offering free education from early childhood through secondary school and have banned child marriage. Sierra Leone and other nations are also working on a new international treaty to support free education and protect children’s rights.

**Impact** – Free education keeps girls in school longer, especially during the ages when they are most at risk of early marriage. Studies show that when lower secondary education is free and required, girls stay in school about 1.6 years longer. Also, countries that guarantee free pre-primary education see fewer child marriages. Sierra Leone’s example shows how political leadership can make a real difference.

**What's next step** – Countries are discussing a new Optional Protocol at the United Nations that would make free education from early childhood through secondary school a legal right worldwide. Negotiations will continue until 2027. Meanwhile, Sierra Leone and 14 other countries are gathering experts and leaders in Geneva to support this cause and push for stronger global laws.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Offering free education from early childhood to secondary school is a proven way to reduce child marriage and improve girls’ futures worldwide.
articles.personality_title_fr: L’éducation gratuite, un moyen efficace pour lutter contre le mariage des enfants
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Chaque année, 12 millions de filles dans le monde sont mariées avant leur 18e anniversaire. Ce mariage précoce prive ces filles de leur enfance et de leurs chances d’apprendre et de grandir. Pour y remédier, le 27 novembre a été déclaré Journée internationale pour l’élimination du mariage des enfants.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Les experts affirment que l’éducation gratuite est un moyen essentiel de réduire le mariage des enfants. Si toutes les filles terminaient le secondaire, le mariage précoce pourrait diminuer de deux tiers. Mais beaucoup de familles ne peuvent pas payer les frais de scolarité, les uniformes ou les livres. Certains pays, comme la Sierra Leone, offrent une éducation gratuite de la petite enfance au secondaire et ont interdit le mariage des enfants. La Sierra Leone et d’autres pays travaillent aussi sur un nouveau traité international pour soutenir l’éducation gratuite et protéger les droits des enfants.

**Impact** – L’éducation gratuite permet aux filles de rester plus longtemps à l’école, surtout à l’âge où elles risquent le plus d’être mariées tôt. Les études montrent que lorsque le secondaire inférieur est gratuit et obligatoire, les filles restent environ 1,6 année de plus à l’école. De plus, les pays qui garantissent une éducation préscolaire gratuite ont moins de mariages d’enfants. L’exemple de la Sierra Leone montre que le leadership politique peut vraiment changer les choses.

**Prochaine étape** – Les pays discutent d’un nouveau Protocole facultatif aux Nations Unies qui rendrait l’éducation gratuite de la petite enfance au secondaire un droit légal dans le monde entier. Les négociations dureront jusqu’en 2027. Pendant ce temps, la Sierra Leone et 14 autres pays rassemblent experts et dirigeants à Genève pour soutenir cette cause et renforcer les lois mondiales.

**Phrase clé** – Offrir une éducation gratuite de la petite enfance au secondaire est un moyen prouvé de réduire le mariage des enfants et d’améliorer l’avenir des filles dans le monde.
articles.personality_title_es: La educación gratuita ayuda a frenar el matrimonio infantil, según nuevo esfuerzo global
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Cada año, 12 millones de niñas en todo el mundo se casan antes de cumplir 18 años. Este matrimonio infantil les quita su infancia y oportunidades para aprender y crecer. Para combatir esto, el 27 de noviembre fue declarado el Día Internacional para la Eliminación del Matrimonio Infantil, Temprano y Forzado.

**Qué pasó** – Los expertos dicen que la educación gratuita es una forma clave de reducir el matrimonio infantil. Si todas las niñas completaran la educación secundaria, el matrimonio infantil podría disminuir en dos tercios. Pero muchas familias no pueden pagar los costos escolares como matrículas, uniformes o libros. Algunos países, como Sierra Leona, han empezado a ofrecer educación gratuita desde la primera infancia hasta la secundaria y han prohibido el matrimonio infantil. Sierra Leona y otros países también están trabajando en un nuevo tratado internacional para apoyar la educación gratuita y proteger los derechos de los niños.

**Impacto** – La educación gratuita mantiene a las niñas en la escuela más tiempo, especialmente en las edades en que corren más riesgo de casarse temprano. Los estudios muestran que cuando la educación secundaria baja es gratuita y obligatoria, las niñas permanecen en la escuela 1.6 años más. Además, los países que garantizan educación preescolar gratuita tienen menos matrimonios infantiles. El ejemplo de Sierra Leona muestra cómo el liderazgo político puede lograr un cambio real.

**Próximo paso** – Los países están discutiendo un nuevo Protocolo Opcional en las Naciones Unidas que haría que la educación gratuita desde la primera infancia hasta la secundaria sea un derecho legal en todo el mundo. Las negociaciones continuarán hasta 2027. Mientras tanto, Sierra Leona y otros 14 países reúnen a expertos y líderes en Ginebra para apoyar esta causa y promover leyes globales más fuertes.

**Frase clave** – Ofrecer educación gratuita desde la primera infancia hasta la secundaria es una forma comprobada de reducir el matrimonio infantil y mejorar el futuro de las niñas en todo el mundo.

articles.title: Putting survivors at the centre of gender-based violence services
articles.summary: Reaching out for help can be an enormous step for survivors of gender-based violence (GBV), and what happens after walking through the doors of a support service can shape the path towards recovery and safety
articles.content:
“More than anything, they want to be believed,” said Erin Gerber, a GBV response specialist with the UN reproductive and sexual health agency, UNFPA, based in Nairobi.

“That was something that came up over and over again.”

Acknowledging survivors’ experiences and ensuring they receive safe and quality support is at the heart of Women at the Centre, UNFPA’s first global GBV case management programme.

Currently implemented in Azerbaijan, El Salvador, Indonesia, Madagascar and Zimbabwe, it aims to strengthen the services survivors receive while building a consistent and professional social service workforce.

Reaching those left out

The programme began by examining existing services and identifying barriers to accessing them.

Assessments pointed to seven marginalized groups that have historically faced discrimination or exclusion, including adolescent girls, older women, LGBTIQ+ survivors, persons with disabilities, people of African descent, Indigenous People, and sex workers.

Across those groups, accessibility, institutional violence, and not being believed were repeated concerns.

For survivors who do reach services, Ms. Gerber explained that quality care begins with seemingly simple things: being welcomed, communicating in their own language, and knowing their information will remain confidential.

Survivors also need to feel physically and emotionally safe, have their decisions respected and, crucially, be genuinely listened to.

Soundcloud

Building a workforce survivors can rely on

A central part of Women at the Centre is strengthening and professionalizing the people providing this support. Investment in GBV response has traditionally focused on health and legal services, while the social service workforce has received less recognition, Ms. Gerber said.

The programme is strengthening training and developing accreditation pathways for caseworkers, helping to build a workforce equipped to provide consistent support and connect survivors with the services they need.

For Ms. Gerber, strengthening the workforce ultimately means ensuring survivors can rely on the care they receive.

“A survivor can get the same quality of care at any time, at any location, whenever they need it. That’s what our goal is,” she said.

Adapting support to communities

While the principles of quality case management remain the same, support must also reflect the communities being served.

In rural Zimbabwe, Ms. Gerber saw how mobile one-stop crisis centres are bringing services closer to women who previously struggled to reach them. Moving between communities, the centres provide information about available support while also helping people identify forms of gender-based violence that may have become normalized or gone unrecognized.

In El Salvador, Women at the Centre works with older women to reflect on their own experiences of violence and how these shape their responses to others. They are then trained to raise awareness, respond to disclosures and connect survivors with support, linking prevention and response within their communities.

The approach differs in each context, but the goal remains the same: making quality support more accessible to survivors.

Eye on the future

For Ms. Gerber, success ultimately comes down to what happens when a survivor seeks help.

“My hope would be that you're walking into a facility and you are seeing an accurate representation of case workers reflected in the survivors and communities who need the services most.”

Where a survivor lives or who they are should not determine the quality of care available to them. It is an ambitious vision, Ms. Gerber acknowledged, but one with a simple goal of “more services for more people who haven’t had them before.”
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories

articles.personality_title: UN program improves support for survivors of gender-based violence worldwide
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many people who suffer from gender-based violence (GBV) find it hard to ask for help. Even when they do, the support they get can affect how well they recover and stay safe.

**What happened** – The United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) started a program called Women at the Centre. It works in countries like Azerbaijan, El Salvador, Indonesia, Madagascar, and Zimbabwe. The program focuses on making sure survivors are believed and treated with respect. It also trains social workers to provide better and consistent help.

**Impact** – The program pays special attention to groups that often face extra challenges, such as young girls, older women, people with disabilities, and LGBTIQ+ individuals. It helps survivors feel safe, listened to, and supported in their own language. Mobile crisis centers in rural areas and community training in places like El Salvador make services easier to reach and understand.

**What’s next step** – UNFPA plans to keep improving the training and professional status of social workers so survivors can get the same good care anywhere and anytime. They also want the workers to reflect the communities they serve, making support more personal and effective.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The Women at the Centre program is making gender-based violence support fairer and stronger by focusing on survivors’ needs and improving the people who help them.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un programme de l’ONU améliore le soutien aux survivants de violences basées sur le genre dans le monde
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Beaucoup de personnes victimes de violences basées sur le genre (VBG) ont du mal à demander de l’aide. Même lorsqu’elles le font, le soutien reçu influence leur rétablissement et leur sécurité.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le Fonds des Nations Unies pour la population (UNFPA) a lancé un programme nommé Women at the Centre. Il est actif dans des pays comme l’Azerbaïdjan, le Salvador, l’Indonésie, Madagascar et le Zimbabwe. Ce programme vise à croire les survivants et à les traiter avec respect. Il forme aussi les travailleurs sociaux pour offrir un meilleur accompagnement.

**Impact** – Le programme cible particulièrement des groupes souvent marginalisés, tels que les jeunes filles, les femmes âgées, les personnes en situation de handicap et les personnes LGBTIQ+. Il aide les survivants à se sentir en sécurité, écoutés et soutenus dans leur propre langue. Des centres mobiles en zones rurales et des formations communautaires au Salvador facilitent l’accès et la compréhension des services.

**Étape suivante** – L’UNFPA souhaite continuer à améliorer la formation et la reconnaissance professionnelle des travailleurs sociaux pour que chaque survivant puisse recevoir la même qualité de soin, partout et à tout moment. Ils veulent aussi que ces travailleurs reflètent les communautés qu’ils servent, rendant le soutien plus personnel et efficace.

**Une phrase clé** – Le programme Women at the Centre rend le soutien aux victimes de violences basées sur le genre plus juste et plus solide en se concentrant sur leurs besoins et en renforçant les personnes qui les accompagnent.
articles.personality_title_es: Programa de la ONU mejora el apoyo a sobrevivientes de violencia de género en todo el mundo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchas personas que sufren violencia de género (VG) tienen dificultades para pedir ayuda. Incluso cuando lo hacen, el apoyo que reciben afecta su recuperación y seguridad.

**Qué pasó** – El Fondo de Población de las Naciones Unidas (UNFPA) lanzó un programa llamado Women at the Centre. Funciona en países como Azerbaiyán, El Salvador, Indonesia, Madagascar y Zimbabue. El programa se centra en creer a las sobrevivientes y tratarlas con respeto. También capacita a trabajadores sociales para ofrecer mejor y constante ayuda.

**Impacto** – El programa presta atención especial a grupos que enfrentan desafíos extras, como niñas, mujeres mayores, personas con discapacidades y personas LGBTIQ+. Ayuda a las sobrevivientes a sentirse seguras, escuchadas y apoyadas en su propio idioma. Centros móviles en áreas rurales y capacitación comunitaria en El Salvador hacen que los servicios sean más accesibles y comprensibles.

**Próximo paso** – UNFPA planea seguir mejorando la capacitación y el reconocimiento profesional de los trabajadores sociales para que las sobrevivientes reciban la misma buena atención en cualquier lugar y momento. También quieren que los trabajadores reflejen a las comunidades que sirven, haciendo el apoyo más personal y efectivo.

**Una frase clave** – El programa Women at the Centre hace que el apoyo a la violencia de género sea más justo y fuerte al enfocarse en las necesidades de las sobrevivientes y mejorar a quienes las ayudan.

articles.title: 'I wouldn't be here today without you': Student's praise for man who stopped Huntingdon train attacker
articles.summary: Astrid credits Stephen Crean with saving her life during the Huntingdon train attack last year.
articles.content:
Meeting after the guilty verdicts were delivered, the two train passengers hugged.

Astrid told the Nottingham Forest fan, who had been travelling home from a match: "It's brilliant to meet you... now we will know each other for a long time."

Crean said: "It means the world to me to meet her. Meeting her was the best thing, it was worth waiting for. I'm just so happy."

Astrid, who did not want to use her last name, said Crean was a hero for his actions that day.

"I just owe him everything," she said, before adding: "I wouldn't be here today without you, and to put your life on the line for someone else, a complete stranger, is just complete bravery."

She said Crean had a "split second to make a decision" and she owed him her life because of that.

"So I'd just like to say thank you," she said.

Crean praised her for alerting him to the danger of Williams as she ran past.

"You can be proud of yourself, and your parents will be proud of you," he added.

During the trial, Crean told the court he decided "to try to stop" the attack and "launched himself towards and at" Williams.

Crean and Astrid both faced terrifying moments as Williams rampaged down the train.

Crean said Williams asked, "Do you want to die?" as he stabbed him several times.

Crean then managed to lock himself in a toilet and call 999 telling them what had happened and that he was covered in blood and scared.

He said he remembered seeing Astrid crying with makeup running down her face.

The fashion student said she remembered seeing Crean throw himself at the attacker and put himself between her and Williams so she could escape.

"I was able to shut the door with the rest of the people behind me. If you hadn't been in between us... I have no idea what would have happened if you weren't there, literally in that second."

Astrid had seen an interview with the 62-year-old on the BBC two days after the attack and contacted the BBC to say he was the man on the train who had helped protect her and others.

Only now the trial has finished have they been able to meet.

Crean said he is pleased the jury found Williams guilty of attempting to murder him as he did not believe he should be allowed to get away with the vicious attacks on him and the other passengers.

On Thursday Cambridgeshire police apologised for failings in stopping Williams after another assault the month before the Huntingdon attack.

As well as the train attacks, Williams was found guilty of attempting to murder four other people in separate incidents and will be sentenced at Cambridge Crown Court on 4 and 5 February.

Crean believes more should have been done to prevent these further offences. "I think they should have had him before. He shouldn't have been allowed to go running around like this. And if they'd picked up on it, we'd have had him before."

Having survived the attack, Astrid is running the London marathon for Crimestoppers as part of her efforts to turn around the harrowing situation she found herself in.

She can, she says, because of Stephen Crean's actions. And he has promised to be there for her again: this time on the finish line.

Additional reporting by Rozina Sini
articles.reasoning: The article highlights an inspiring act of bravery where a man risked his life to stop a violent attack, saving others including a student. It emphasizes real-world positive impact by showcasing courage and human solidarity in the face of violence, with the survivor now channeling her experience into a charitable cause. The story has broad societal relevance by promoting heroism, resilience, and crime prevention awareness.
articles.personality_title: Man’s quick action stops Huntingdon train attack, saves student’s life
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Last year, a violent attack happened on a train in Huntingdon. A man named Stephen Crean stepped in to stop the attacker, protecting other passengers including a student named Astrid.

**What happened** – After the attacker was found guilty, Astrid and Stephen met for the first time. Astrid thanked Stephen for risking his life to save her. Stephen had acted quickly, rushing at the attacker to stop him. During the attack, Stephen was stabbed but managed to lock himself in a train toilet and call emergency services. Astrid escaped safely thanks to his bravery.

**Impact** – Stephen’s quick decision and courage saved lives during a dangerous moment. Astrid says she wouldn’t be alive without him. Now, she is running the London marathon to raise money for Crimestoppers, a charity that helps fight crime. Stephen’s actions show how one person’s bravery can protect many others.

**What’s next step** – The attacker will be sentenced soon for multiple crimes. Astrid plans to finish the marathon with Stephen cheering her on. Meanwhile, there are calls for better police action to stop dangerous people earlier, to prevent attacks like this.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A man’s brave act on a train stopped an attacker and saved a student’s life, inspiring her to support crime prevention.

articles.title: DR Congo: Peacekepers step up civilian protection amid fighting in Ituri
articles.summary: United Nations peacekeepers in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have stepped up efforts to protect civilians in Ebola-hit Ituri province following renewed armed clashes in Djugu territory.
articles.content:
The UN mission in the country, MONUSCO, reports that security has significantly deteriorated in several areas due to clashes between Congolese forces and the Convention for the Popular Revolution (CRP), one of dozens of armed groups in the resource-rich east.

The fighting has displaced thousands of people and threatened access to essential health services.

MONUSCO said that heavy fighting had been reported on 18 November around Bule locality and the Savo Plain displacement site which hosts roughly 70,000 people.

“The violence has triggered further population displacement, including among people who had already fled insecurity,” the UN mission said, noting that 24 civilians, mostly women and children, had sought refuge with its peacekeepers in Bayoo.

Trapped health workers evacuated

Clashes and displacement in the Akwe, Damas and Mbidjo areas prompted MONUSCO’s Bangladeshi Rapid Deployment Battalion (BANRDB) to strengthen its presence on the ground and provide assistance to people in need, particularly healthcare workers.

As a result, peacekeepers were able to evacuate 10 health workers from the Akwe General Referral Hospital on Tuesday, where they had been sheltering for over three days.

“These healthcare workers, who are actively involved in the response to the Ebola outbreak, play a vital role in assisting communities already weakened by violence and displacement,” MONUSCO said.

Supporting Ebola response

The rescue operation had faced significant logistical challenges as the peacekeepers were forced to abandon their initial planned route due to difficult terrain, poor road conditions and a wooden bridge deemed too fragile to cross.

“This intervention is part of MONUSCO’s support for Ebola response efforts, particularly through the protection of healthcare personnel and the facilitation of safe access to healthcare for populations affected by violence,” the mission said.

MONUSCO noted that just four days earlier, Bangladeshi and Nepalese peacekeepers had facilitated the safe return of 380 civilians from Fataki locality to the Savo Plain displacement site after clashes had forced them to flee.

The mission has also increased patrols in the area to protect civilians from violence on the part of armed groups.
